claim: C. elegans has 302 neurons in hermaphrodites.
source: C. elegans is one of the simplest multicellular organisms with only 302 neurons in hermaphrodites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans anatomy.

claim: The behavioral screening approach in C. elegans neuroscience is performed at a different hierarchical level than the level at which perturbations are applied.
source: Although proven to be effective, this approach is far from ideal because the behavioral screening is performed in a different hierarchical level than the level at which the perturbation was initially applied (Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999.

claim: Pan-neuronal activities in moving worms can be recorded using spinning disk confocal microscopy.
source: More recent work describes methods to record pan-neuronal activities in moving worms using spinning disk confocal microscopy (Venkatachalam et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Venkatachalam et al., 2016.

claim: AWC neurons are amphid sensory neurons located in the head region of C. elegans.
source: AWCs are the amphid sensory neurons located in the head region of C. elegans, and are crucial for the sensing of certain volatile chemicals.
evidence: This is established knowledge about AWC neuron location and function.

claim: AWC neurons are functionally asymmetric.
source: Unlike most other pair-wise neurons, AWC neurons are functionally asymmetric: the AWCON neuron senses butanone odor, and AWCOFF senses 2,3-pentanedione, while both neurons symmetrically sense benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol (Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007), which are essential for proper chemotaxis (Clark et al., 2006; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007; Clark et al., 2006; Mori and Ohshima, 1995.

claim: AWCON neuron senses butanone odor.
source: Unlike most other pair-wise neurons, AWC neurons are functionally asymmetric: the AWCON neuron senses butanone odor, and AWCOFF senses 2,3-pentanedione, while both neurons symmetrically sense benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol (Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007), which are essential for proper chemotaxis (Clark et al., 2006; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: AWCOFF neuron senses 2,3-pentanedione.
source: Unlike most other pair-wise neurons, AWC neurons are functionally asymmetric: the AWCON neuron senses butanone odor, and AWCOFF senses 2,3-pentanedione, while both neurons symmetrically sense benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol (Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007), which are essential for proper chemotaxis (Clark et al., 2006; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: Both AWC neurons symmetrically sense benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol.
source: Unlike most other pair-wise neurons, AWC neurons are functionally asymmetric: the AWCON neuron senses butanone odor, and AWCOFF senses 2,3-pentanedione, while both neurons symmetrically sense benzaldehyde and isoamyl alcohol (Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007), which are essential for proper chemotaxis (Clark et al., 2006; Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wes and Bargmann, 2001; Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: AFD is the primary sensory neuron for thermotaxis.
source: In thermosensation, AFD is the primary sensory neuron and is essential for thermotaxis (Mori and Ohshima, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mori and Ohshima, 1995.

claim: AWC exhibits AFD-like continuous calcium transients in temperature ramps with thresholds dependent on previously exposed temperature.
source: One group reports that AWC exhibits AFD-like continuous calcium transients in temperature ramps, and that its thresholds depend on the previously exposed temperature (Kuhara et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuhara et al., 2008.

claim: AWC calcium transients consist of short stochastic transients whose frequency responds to previous temperature.
source: Another group also reports AWC's role in thermosensation but their calcium transients are more similar to interneuron AIY signaling (Figure 2B), in the way that they consist of short stochastic transients whose frequency responds to the previous temperature (Biron et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biron et al., 2008.

claim: No membrane current was detected in AWC neurons during thermal ramps in an electrophysiological study.
source: Also there is an electrophysiological study which detected no membrane current in AWC neurons in the thermal ramps (Ramot et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramot et al., 2008.

claim: Removal of AWC by laser ablation or cell-specific recCaspase expression results in no significant disruption in positive or negative thermotaxis.
source: A more recent study states that removal of AWC by laser ablation or cell-specific recCaspase expression results in no significant disruption either in positive or negative thermotaxis (Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2014.

claim: Calcium transients in AWCOFF neurons are positively correlated to nociceptive thermal stimuli.
source: This novel activity was then tested in freely moving animals in which the nociceptive stimulation was applied to further investigate their role in physiological behaviors utilizing asymmetry mutants and laser ablation of AWCs. Indeed, the thermal avoidance behavior, which has been linked to the activities in the AFD, FLP, PVD, and PHC neurons (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012; Mohammadi et al., 2013) is also strongly coupled to the AWCOFF neurons but not AWCON.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript and citations.

claim: Calcium transients in AWCON neurons are negatively correlated to nociceptive thermal stimuli.
source: However, when we applied either a very fast temperature rise (a few degrees in less than 50 ms) or high absolute temperature (33°C), we detected very deterministic AWC signals that are asymmetric in AWCON and AWCOFF: the calcium transients in AWCOFF neurons are always positively correlated to the nociceptive thermal stimuli whereas the transients in AWCON neurons are negatively correlated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Thermal avoidance behavior has been linked to activities in AFD, FLP, PVD, and PHC neurons.
source: Indeed, the thermal avoidance behavior, which has been linked to the activities in the AFD, FLP, PVD, and PHC neurons (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012; Mohammadi et al., 2013) is also strongly coupled to the AWCOFF neurons but not AWCON.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2012; Mohammadi et al., 2013.

claim: AWCOFF neuron is essential and sufficient for noxious heat sensation and subsequent avoidance behavior.
source: By combining pan-neuronal calcium imaging with our novel behavioral analyses, we found that the AWCOFF neuron is essential and sufficient for noxious heat sensation and the subsequent avoidance behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging and behavioral assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The imaging system utilizes wide-field illumination with post-acquisition deconvolution rather than confocal optics.
source: The system utilizes wide-field illumination with post-acquisition deconvolution rather than confocal optics, allowing for very efficient collection of fluorescence in multiple optical planes.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: The imaging system enables fast acquisition of pan-neuronal images at 20 fps with minimal photo-toxicity and photo-bleaching for up to 45 min.
source: This combination has enabled fast acquisition of pan-neuronal images (20 fps) with minimal photo-toxicity and photo-bleaching (up to 45 min acquisition, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) using conventional calcium indicators expressed in the neurons of C. elegans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nuclear-targeted indicators were used because the small size and compactness of the C. elegans nervous system makes whole neuron segmentation very difficult.
source: As previously reported (Schrödel et al., 2013), we used nuclear-targeted indicators because the small size and compactness of the C. elegans nervous system makes whole neuron segmentation very difficult.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schrödel et al., 2013 and reasoning about technical challenges.

claim: Ratiometric indicator was critical for stable measurement of neural activities due to motion artifacts.
source: Due to some motion artifacts, the ratiometric indicator was critical for the stable measurement of neural activities.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claim: Strong calcium signals were detected in the nuclei of AFD thermosensory neurons during gradual temperature increase.
source: As previously reported (Clark et al., 2006), we detected very strong and deterministic signals in the nuclei of AFD thermosensory neurons, when we gradually increased the worm's temperature, consistent with a dependence on the cultivation temperature (TC) (Figure 1C, top, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Clark et al., 2006.

claim: AFD calcium signals are dependent on cultivation temperature.
source: As previously reported (Clark et al., 2006), we detected very strong and deterministic signals in the nuclei of AFD thermosensory neurons, when we gradually increased the worm's temperature, consistent with a dependence on the cultivation temperature (TC) (Figure 1C, top, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and citation to Clark et al., 2006.

claim: Similar but smaller signals were detected from the nuclei of AIY interneurons during temperature increase.
source: We also detected similar but smaller signals from the nuclei of AIY interneurons (Figure 1C, second), as shown previously, confirming the efficacy of this approach (Clark et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and citation to Clark et al., 2006.

claim: RIS neuron signals are broad, less consistent, but dependent on previously exposed temperature on average, starting to rise about 3°C above the cultivation temperature.
source: Unlike AFD or AIY neurons, the signals from the RIS neuron are broad and less consistent, but they are nonetheless dependent on the previously exposed temperature on average, and start to rise about 3°C above the TC (Figure 1C, third).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: RIS neuron has been previously linked to quiescence but not thermosensation.
source: One notable neuron was the GABAergic RIS neuron, which previously has been linked to quiescence but not thermosensation (Turek et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Turek et al., 2013.

claim: RMDV and SMDV neurons showed negative correlation to AFD or RIS activity.
source: RIS is one example in this screening, and there were other neurons such as RMDV and SMDV, which showed negative correlation to the AFD or RIS activity (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Thermal nociception and thermotaxis involve mostly separate signaling pathways in C. elegans.
source: Thermal nociception and thermotaxis involve mostly separate signaling pathways in C. elegans (Glauser et al., 2011; Wittenburg and Baumeister, 1999) but the circuitry of thermal nociception is not as well understood, so we next sought to identify novel neural functions in response to noxious thermal stimuli.
evidence: Supported by citations to Glauser et al., 2011; Wittenburg and Baumeister, 1999.

claim: A focused infrared laser at 1440 nm was used to rapidly heat the head region of C. elegans from 23°C to 33°C within a few tens of milliseconds.
source: Instead of a thermoelectric heat pump, we used a focused infrared laser (1440 nm) to rapidly heat up the head region of C. elegans. The laser beam was carefully controlled so that the local temperature rises from 23°C to 33°C within a few tens of milliseconds and held for 20 s with an interstimulus interval (ISI) of 30 s.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used.

claim: Both left and right AFD neurons showed the most distinct calcium signals with strong positive correlation to noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Similar to our thermosensory measurements, both the left and right AFD neurons showed the most distinct calcium signals with strong positive correlation to the noxious thermal stimuli (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: FLP sensory neurons and AIY thermotactic interneurons had positive correlation to noxious thermal stimuli with reduced signal strength.
source: Other sensory neurons such as FLP and thermotactic interneurons such as AIY also had positive correlation, albeit with reduced signal strength (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Noxious thermal stimuli did not consistently invoke signals in RIS, RMDV, and SMDV neurons.
source: In contrast to the thermal ramp stimulation, the noxious thermal stimuli did not consistently invoke signals in the aforementioned RIS, RMDV, and SMDV neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations comparing different stimulation protocols.

claim: One AWC neuron produced a deterministic positive signal that showed adaptation to repeated heating.
source: One of the AWC neurons produced a deterministic, positive signal, and showed adaptation to repeated heating in a similar fashion to what we measured in AFD.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging.

claim: The other AWC neuron produced a deterministic negative signal that did not adapt.
source: While the other AWC neuron produced a deterministic negative signal that did not adapt.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging.

claim: AWC neurons have been previously implicated in chemosensation and thermosensation, but not in noxious thermosensation.
source: AWC neurons previously have been implicated in chemosensation (Bargmann et al., 1993) and thermosensation (Kuhara et al., 2008; Biron et al., 2008), but not in noxious thermosensation.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bargmann et al., 1993; Kuhara et al., 2008; Biron et al., 2008.

claim: AWCOFF signaling was positively correlated with noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Calcium imaging of the transgenic strain revealed that the AWCOFF signaling was positively correlated with the stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, middle), while AWCON signaling was negatively correlated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AWCON signaling was negatively correlated with noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Calcium imaging of the transgenic strain revealed that the AWCOFF signaling was positively correlated with the stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, middle), while AWCON signaling was negatively correlated (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, top).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitude of AWCOFF signals adapted with repeated stimuli, similar to AFD neurons.
source: The amplitude of AWCOFF signals adapted (Figure 2C, top) with repeated stimuli, similar to the calcium signals in AFD neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom), but the signals in AWCON did not show a pattern of adaptation (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AWCON signals did not show a pattern of adaptation to repeated stimuli.
source: The amplitude of AWCOFF signals adapted (Figure 2C, top) with repeated stimuli, similar to the calcium signals in AFD neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, bottom), but the signals in AWCON did not show a pattern of adaptation (Figure 2C, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In nsy-1 mutants, both AWCs become AWCON-like.
source: These strains have cell-fate deficiencies with both AWCs becoming AWCON-like in nsy-1, and AWCOFF-like in nsy-7 (Lesch et al., 2009; Troemel et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lesch et al., 2009; Troemel et al., 1999.

claim: In nsy-7 mutants, both AWCs become AWCOFF-like.
source: These strains have cell-fate deficiencies with both AWCs becoming AWCON-like in nsy-1, and AWCOFF-like in nsy-7 (Lesch et al., 2009; Troemel et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lesch et al., 2009; Troemel et al., 1999.

claim: Both AWC neurons in nsy-1 mutants correlated negatively with noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Calcium imaging in these mutants showed clear disruption of the functional asymmetry in response to the noxious stimulation. Both AWC neurons in nsy-1 correlated negatively with the stimuli (Figure 3A) while both AWCs in nsy-7 correlated positively (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both AWC neurons in nsy-7 mutants correlated positively with noxious thermal stimuli.
source: Calcium imaging in these mutants showed clear disruption of the functional asymmetry in response to the noxious stimulation. Both AWC neurons in nsy-1 correlated negatively with the stimuli (Figure 3A) while both AWCs in nsy-7 correlated positively (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Calcium transients in AFD neurons did not have any abnormality in nsy-1 or nsy-7 mutants.
source: Calcium transients in AFD neurons did not have any abnormality in either of the mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The fractions of worms performing forward and reversal behaviors during the first heating phase in nsy-1 and nsy-7 mutants did not show significant difference from N2 wild-type.
source: The fractions of worms performing the forward (Figure 4A, left) and reversal behaviors (Figure 4A, middle) during the first heating phase in both mutants did not show any significant difference from that of N2 wild-type; however, the fraction of turning behavior in the nsy-1 mutant but not for nsy-7 was significantly reduced (Figure 4A, right) suggesting a role of the AWCOFF neuron in avoidance behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The fraction of turning behavior in nsy-1 mutant was significantly reduced compared to N2 wild-type during the first heating phase.
source: The fractions of worms performing the forward (Figure 4A, left) and reversal behaviors (Figure 4A, middle) during the first heating phase in both mutants did not show any significant difference from that of N2 wild-type; however, the fraction of turning behavior in the nsy-1 mutant but not for nsy-7 was significantly reduced (Figure 4A, right) suggesting a role of the AWCOFF neuron in avoidance behavior.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a pattern of adaptation in the fractions of turning and reversal behaviors during repeated heating phases in N2 wild-type and nsy-7, but not in nsy-1.
source: We also noticed that there is a pattern of adaptation in the fractions of turning and reversal behaviors during the repeated heating phases in N2 wild-type and nsy-7, but not in nsy-1 (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The behavioral adaptation pattern matches the pattern of calcium transients where AWCOFF but not AWCON showed adaptation.
source: The result matches the pattern of the calcium transients, in which AWCOFF but not AWCON showed a similar pattern of adaptation.
evidence: This is an inference connecting calcium imaging data with behavioral data.

claim: For nsy-1 mutant, the forward-to-reversal transitions during the first heating phase were reduced compared to N2 wild-type and nsy-7.
source: We found that for the nsy-1 mutant, the forward-to-reversal (FR) transitions during the first heating phase were reduced compared to the N2 wild-type and nsy-7 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The nsy-1 mutation affects the reversal-to-forward transition rates.
source: It seems that the nsy-1 mutation also affects the reversal-to-forward (RF) transition rates (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), thus resulting in apparently wild-type reversal fraction.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The apparent reduction of turn fraction in nsy-1 is due to balanced reduction in both FR and reversal-to-turn transitions.
source: The graphs indicate that the apparent reduction of the turn fraction in nsy-1 is due to the balanced reduction in both the FR and the reversal-to-turn (RT) transitions.
evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of behavioral transition data.

claim: The apparent similarity in reversal fraction in nsy-1 is the result of reduction in both FR and RF transitions.
source: Likewise, the apparent similarity in the reversal fraction in nsy-1 is the result of the reduction in both the FR and the RF transition as mentioned above.
evidence: This is an inference based on analysis of behavioral transition data.

claim: The nsy-1 mutation did not significantly affect the turn-to-forward transition.
source: The nsy-1 mutation did not significantly affect the turn-to-forward (TF) transition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral analysis.

claim: FR transition rates in N2 and nsy-7 adapt over repeated heating phases, but not for nsy-1 mutant.
source: Another interesting feature of the transitions is that the FR transition rates in N2 and nsy-7 adapt over the repeated heating phases, but not for the nsy-1 mutant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral analysis.

claim: The adaptation pattern in FR transitions is similar to the adaptation pattern of calcium transients in AWC neurons.
source: This pattern is present only in the FR transitions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) and is similar to the adaptation pattern of the calcium transients in AWC neurons where AWCOFF neurons displayed significant adaptation but not the AWCON-like neurons.
evidence: This is an inference connecting calcium imaging data with behavioral data, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: AWCOFF neuron is responsible for the accelerated FR transition rate during noxious heating and for its adaptation to repeated heating stimuli.
source: These results imply that the AWCOFF neuron is responsible for the accelerated FR transition rate during the noxious heating, and for its adaptation to repeated heating stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on combined calcium imaging and behavioral data.

claim: The nsy-1 mutant displayed a 5-fold reduction in mean reversal duration compared to wild-type after noxious thermal stimulation.
source: Compared to the wild-type, the nsy-1 mutant that does not have functional AWCOFF neurons displayed a 5-fold reduction in mean reversal duration, whereas the nsy-7 mutant that do carry functional AWCOFF neurons maintained a similar reversal duration (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The nsy-7 mutant maintained similar reversal duration to wild-type after noxious thermal stimulation.
source: Compared to the wild-type, the nsy-1 mutant that does not have functional AWCOFF neurons displayed a 5-fold reduction in mean reversal duration, whereas the nsy-7 mutant that do carry functional AWCOFF neurons maintained a similar reversal duration (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The reduction in reversal duration in nsy-1 was reverted by increasing the laser current to 150 mA.
source: Interestingly, the reduction in the reversal duration in nsy-1 was reverted by increasing the laser current to 150 mA suggesting that the avoidance behavior is triggered either by a mechanism involving a nociceptive threshold, which is higher in the AWCON-like neurons, or by other signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from behavioral assays.

claim: Ablating AWCON neuron did not significantly alter the reversal duration after noxious thermal stimulation at 50 mA.
source: As expected, we observed that ablating the AWCON neuron did not significantly alter the reversal duration after the stimulation at 50 mA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from laser ablation experiments.

claim: Ablating either AWCOFF or both AWCs significantly reduced the reversal duration after noxious thermal stimulation.
source: However, ablating either AWCOFF or both AWCs significantly reduced the reversal duration immediately after the stimulation (Figure 5B), confirming that the AWCOFF neuron is required and sufficient for noxious thermal avoidance following the stimulation with the conditions described above.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AWCOFF neuron is required and sufficient for noxious thermal avoidance following stimulation at 50 mA.
source: However, ablating either AWCOFF or both AWCs significantly reduced the reversal duration immediately after the stimulation (Figure 5B), confirming that the AWCOFF neuron is required and sufficient for noxious thermal avoidance following the stimulation with the conditions described above.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: At higher laser currents, worms with AWCOFF or both AWCs ablated increased their reversal duration, suggesting the presence of another thermal nociceptive signaling pathway.
source: At higher laser currents, worms with the AWCOFF neuron or both AWCON/AWCOFF neurons ablated increased their reversal duration, suggesting the likely presence of another thermal nociceptive signaling pathway.
evidence: This is speculation based on experimental observations at different laser intensities.

claim: In olfactory functions, AWCOFF was implicated in detecting the removal of attractive odor and activating local search behavior consisting of reversal and omega turns.
source: In the previous studies concerning olfactory functions in AWC neurons, AWCOFF was implicated in detecting the removal of attractive odor, and in activating a local search behavior consisting of reversal and omega turns (Chalasani et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chalasani et al., 2007.

claim: In both olfactory and nociceptive sensation, AWCOFF is required for reversal locomotion and omega turns.
source: Our findings are in good agreement with the previous ones in that both in the olfactory and nociceptive sensation, AWCOFF is required for reversal locomotion and omega turns.
evidence: This is an inference connecting current findings with previous literature.

claim: The pan-neuronal approach can map most of the previously reported thermosensation circuitry in a single screening.
source: As we have demonstrated in this study, the pan-neuronal approach can be very efficient in that we were able to map most of the previously reported thermosensation circuitry in a single screening.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented.

claim: The pan-neuronal approach identified previously unidentified neurons such as RIS for thermosensation and AWC asymmetry for thermal nociception.
source: Moreover, we also identified previously unidentified neurons such as RIS for thermosensation and AWC asymmetry for thermal nociception.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental results presented.

claim: AWCOFF neuron plays a critical role in sensing and/or processing thermal nociception in the central nervous system of C. elegans.
source: The behavioral assay results of the nsy-1 mutant and AWCOFF ablated worms, suggest that the AWCOFF neuron plays a critical role in sensing and/or processing thermal nociception in the central nervous system of C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference based on combined behavioral and ablation data.

claim: The imaging system uses a 1440 nm wavelength to selectively heat water molecules without directly stimulating other biomolecules in the tissue.
source: We chose the wavelength to selectively heat up water molecules without directly stimulating any other biomolecules in the tissue (Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Smith et al., 2009.

claim: A 100 ms laser pulse at 50 mA heats a small region (150 µm) approximately 1.2°C above ambient temperature (23°C).
source: A 100 ms laser pulse (50 mA) heats a small region (150 µm) ~1.2°C above the ambient temperature (23°C).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental parameters used.

claim: A heating pulse to the head region causes a deterministic noxious avoidance response: a long reversal locomotion usually followed by an omega turn.
source: A heating pulse with these parameters to the head region of a worm causes a deterministic noxious avoidance response: a long reversal locomotion usually followed by an omega turn.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Most worms survived the calcium imaging conditions and showed no behavioral defect a few hours after being transferred back to an NGM plate.
source: Most of the worms survived this condition and showed no behavioral defect a few hours after they were transferred back to an NGM plate.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: The imaging system utilizes GPU-based 3D deconvolution for image processing.
source: In order to investigate the calcium dynamics in the nervous system of C. elegans, we have developed an imaging system with fast z-scan, multicolor, and thermal stimulation capabilities, along with a software package for automated system operation, image registration, cellular segmentation, gradient vector field (GVF)-based cell tracking (Li et al., 2007), and GPU-based 3D deconvolution (Bruce and Butte, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruce and Butte, 2013.

claim: The imaging system uses gradient vector field (GVF)-based cell tracking.
source: In order to investigate the calcium dynamics in the nervous system of C. elegans, we have developed an imaging system with fast z-scan, multicolor, and thermal stimulation capabilities, along with a software package for automated system operation, image registration, cellular segmentation, gradient vector field (GVF)-based cell tracking (Li et al., 2007), and GPU-based 3D deconvolution (Bruce and Butte, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2007.

claim: Nuclear-localized calcium indicators miss functional signals located in the cytoplasm far distal to the cell body.
source: Also, our pan-neuronal calcium indicators are localized only to the nuclei and so we miss a number of functional signals that are located in the cytoplasm, perhaps far distal to the cell body.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged based on the experimental design.

claim: Strong calcium signals were not detected in the nuclei of some interneurons such as RIA.
source: Using this imaging strategy (see Materials and methods), we detected strong calcium signals in the nuclei of the command, motor, and sensory neurons (Figure 1B), but not in the nuclei of some interneurons such as RIA, which is in agreement with previous reports where the signals were detected in the neurites and cell body, but not in the nucleus (Hendricks et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citation to Hendricks et al., 2012.

claim: Signals in RIA interneuron were detected in neurites and cell body but not in the nucleus in previous reports.
source: Using this imaging strategy (see Materials and methods), we detected strong calcium signals in the nuclei of the command, motor, and sensory neurons (Figure 1B), but not in the nuclei of some interneurons such as RIA, which is in agreement with previous reports where the signals were detected in the neurites and cell body, but not in the nucleus (Hendricks et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hendricks et al., 2012.
